conventional_description: In Western medicine, excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) is categorized as primary, often localized to palms, soles, or underarms, or secondary to conditions like hyperthyroidism, menopause, or infections. Diagnosis typically involves a physical exam and sometimes a starch-iodine test to map sweat areas. Treatment ranges from antiperspirants to Botox or surgery.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatments usually start with clinical-strength antiperspirants. If those fail, options include iontophoresis (using water to conduct a mild electrical current), Botox injections to block nerve signals, oral anticholinergic medications, and in severe cases, surgery such as endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy (ETS). Each has its own benefits and limitations.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views sweating as a delicate balance between the body's defensive shield (Wei Qi) and its internal fluids. The Lungs and Spleen govern Wei Qi, which controls the opening and closing of pores. The Kidneys anchor Yin and Yang, the cooling and warming forces that regulate body temperature. When any of these systems is out of balance, sweat can leak out at the wrong time or in the wrong way.
The timing of sweat is often the first clue. Spontaneous sweating during the day, especially with the slightest activity, points to a weakness in the Wei Qi - the shield is too thin to hold fluids in. Night sweats that soak the pillow and stop upon waking, however, suggest the body's cooling Yin has run low, allowing empty heat to push fluids out during sleep. This simple distinction already separates two completely different root causes.
The quality of sweat also tells a story. Cold, clammy sweat that leaves you chilled hints at a deeper Yang deficiency, where the body's warming fire is too weak to secure the pores. Sticky, yellow-tinged sweat that feels heavy on the skin signals dampness and heat stewing together internally. When sweat pours out with high fever and raging thirst, a practitioner suspects Bright Yang Stomach Heat - an excess condition where internal fire is steaming fluids outward.
Because so many organ systems and energetic layers can be involved, one Western diagnosis of hyperhidrosis can have many TCM faces. This is why treatment is never one-size-fits-all. A formula that works brilliantly for a person with Yin deficiency night sweats would be completely wrong for someone whose cold, clammy sweat comes from Yang deficiency. TCM's strength lies in matching the pattern, not just the symptom.
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking when the sweating happens and what makes it worse. Spontaneous sweating that appears during the day with even light activity points toward a deficiency of Protective (Wei) Qi, while sweating that soaks the pillow at night and stops upon waking strongly suggests Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat. This simple question about timing already separates the two most common patterns.
If the sweat comes with a distinct aversion to wind, mild body aches, and a feeling that the body cannot regulate its own temperature, the practitioner considers Ying-Wei Disharmony. The tongue often looks pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse feels floating and soft, confirming that the nutritive and defensive energies are out of sync rather than simply weak.
Bright Yang Stomach Heat is suspected when sweating is profuse and accompanied by high fever, intense thirst for cold drinks, and a flushed face. The tongue appears red with a thick yellow coat, and the pulse feels large and forceful. This pattern is about true excess heat deep inside, not a weakness, so the sweating is the body’s attempt to vent that internal fire.
When sweat feels sticky, leaves a yellowish stain on clothing, and comes with a heavy, sluggish sensation in the limbs, Damp-Heat is the likely culprit. The practitioner will look for a greasy yellow tongue coating and a slippery, rapid pulse. This pattern often involves the digestive system, so questions about appetite, bloating, and bowel movements help confirm the diagnosis.
For those who break out in cold, thin sweat even at rest and feel chilled and utterly drained, Yang Deficiency is the key suspect. The tongue is typically pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep and weak. This pattern reflects a deep exhaustion of the body’s warming and holding power, making it unable to keep fluids inside.

patterns.symptoms: ["Spontaneous sweating that worsens with even mild exertion", "Aversion to wind and drafts", "Frequent colds and slow recovery from illness", "Fatigue, low stamina, and a weak, quiet voice", "Pale, slightly puffy complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion, Exposure to wind and drafts, Raw, cold foods, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Rest, Warm, nourishing foods, Gentle exercise, Keeping warm
patterns.why_this_happens: Your Protective (Wei) Qi acts like an invisible shield that wraps around your body and controls your pores. When this shield is weak, the pores cannot close properly, and sweat leaks out at the slightest provocation - even gentle activity pushes it over its limit. Because the Spleen and Lungs are the engines that produce this Qi, you also feel tired and catch colds easily.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy body with possible teeth marks; thin white coat. Pulse: Floating, empty, and soggy (浮虚濡, fú xū rú).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: When Protective Qi is deficient, the body's gates (pores) cannot stay shut. Rest and nourishing food build Qi, while wind and overwork further deplete it. Warmth supports the Yang Qi that holds sweat in, and shielding from drafts prevents the external pathogen from invading the already weakened surface.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews with gentle spices (ginger, cinnamon) to support Qi. Avoid raw, cold foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi builds Qi without exhausting it; overexertion will worsen sweating. Keep the neck and back covered in windy weather.

patterns.symptoms: ["Night sweats that soak the sheets", "Heat sensation in palms, soles, and chest", "Dry mouth and throat, worse in the evening", "Flushed cheekbones", "Restlessness and difficulty staying asleep", "Thirst for small sips of water"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried foods, Alcohol, Overwork and stress, Hot and stuffy environments, Staying up late
patterns.better_with: Cool, quiet bedroom, Sipping water, Eating pears and cucumbers, Going to bed early, Gentle yoga or meditation
patterns.why_this_happens: Yin is the body's cooling and moistening energy. When it runs low, the relative Yang becomes unchecked and generates empty heat, like a pot simmering dry. This heat is most active at night when Yin should naturally be dominant, so it pushes fluids outward as night sweats, especially from the palms, soles, and chest where the heat concentrates.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry, with cracks and little to no coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid, weak on deep pressure.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, moistening reserve. Spicy foods, alcohol, and emotional stress all generate heat and consume Yin, making the internal fire burn hotter and forcing sweat out at night. A hot room or late nights further deplete Yin when it is naturally meant to be restored. Cooling foods and hydration directly replenish Yin and calm the empty heat, while rest and early sleep align with the body's natural cycle of Yin restoration, helping to contain the heat and keep sweat in check.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and overly heating foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which dry out Yin and fuel the internal fire. Instead, eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, cucumber, tofu, and watermelon. Keep your bedroom cool and dark, and establish a calming bedtime routine. Gentle exercise like tai chi or yoga can help, but avoid intense workouts that overheat you. Go to bed early-the hours before midnight are the most replenishing for Yin.

patterns.why_this_happens: The body's protective (Wei) Qi and nutritive (Ying) Qi are meant to work together to keep sweat in and wind out. When they fall out of sync-often after catching a cold or due to a weak constitution-the Wei Qi can no longer hold the pores closed. Wind easily invades, and sweat leaks out, especially with the slightest movement or a draft.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-red or slightly pale body with a thin, white, moist coating. Pulse: floating and moderate (浮缓, fú huǎn) or floating and weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind and cold directly challenge the Wei Qi, making it even harder for the body to keep the pores closed, so sweat pours out. Warmth, rest, and gentle covering help the Wei Qi stabilize and the Ying Qi stay put, restoring the natural balance between the two.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Dress in layers and avoid sitting in drafts. Sip warm ginger tea to support the defensive Qi. Gentle daily movement helps, but don't push to the point of sweating heavily. Keep your neck and upper back covered when it's windy.

patterns.why_this_happens: When intense heat builds in the Stomach, particularly along the Bright Yang channel, it acts like a boiling pot, steaming the body's fluids outward through the pores. This produces drenching sweat that flows freely, but because the source is internal heat rather than a surface imbalance, the sweat does not cool the body or break the fever. The heat also consumes fluids, causing intense thirst and a dry mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with yellow dry coating. Pulse: overflowing and surging (Hong), rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is driven by excess internal heat that steams fluids outward. Cooling measures directly counteract the heat, reducing the force that pushes sweat out. Hot and spicy foods, alcohol, and hot environments add more heat to an already overheated system, making sweating worse. Emotional stress stirs up Yang energy, which can further intensify the fire. Rest and calm allow the body to conserve Yin fluids and prevent overheating.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid hot, spicy, and greasy foods that add fuel to the fire. Eat cooling foods like watermelon, cucumber, pear, and mung bean soup. Drink plenty of water at room temperature. Rest in a cool, well-ventilated space and avoid saunas or hot baths.

patterns.why_this_happens: When dampness and heat combine in the body, they create a steamy internal environment that pushes fluids outward through the skin. This produces sweat that feels sticky and may leave a yellowish stain. The heaviness and greasy tongue coating are tell-tale signs that dampness is the root cause, not just simple overheating.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow, greasy coating that is difficult to scrape off, may be swollen with teeth marks. Pulse: soggy-rapid (Ru Shu) or slippery-rapid (Hua Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-heat thrives on moisture and heat. Humid weather and heavy, greasy foods add to the internal dampness, while spicy foods and alcohol stir up heat, making the body steam even more. Cooling, drying foods and a dry environment help counteract this. Gentle movement encourages Qi circulation and urination, which drains dampness, while frustration and stress can stagnate Qi and worsen heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digestible foods like barley, mung beans, and bitter greens. Avoid greasy, spicy, sweet, and dairy-heavy foods that generate dampness and heat. Stay in a cool, dry environment and wear breathable fabrics. Gentle exercise like walking helps move Qi and drain dampness, but avoid overheating.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Yang is the body’s warming, holding power. When Yang is too weak, it can no longer secure the pores and keep fluids inside. Sweat leaks out easily, and because it lacks the warmth of Yang, the sweat feels cold and clammy.
This kind of sweating often happens at rest or with very little movement, and it leaves the person feeling deeply chilled and drained. It is the body’s way of losing what little Yang it has left.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, and moist with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yang is the body’s fire; cold and overexertion snuff it out, causing more cold sweat. Warmth, rest, and moxibustion gently feed that fire, restoring the body’s ability to hold fluids and stay warm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and use warming spices like ginger and cinnamon. Avoid raw, cold, and icy foods that drain Yang. Keep the body warm, especially the lower back and abdomen, and get gentle daily movement like walking to gradually build Yang without exhausting it.

The name "Jade Windscreen" reflects its role as a precious shield against illness-causing pathogens.

It works by nourishing the body's cooling, moistening fluids (Yin) while clearing excess internal fire from all three body regions, and strengthening the body's surface defenses to stop the sweating. Li Dongyuan called it the "sage remedy for night sweats."

formulas.translation: Cinnamon Twig Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Releases the Muscle Layer, Harmonizes the Nutritive and Defensive Qi, Disperses Wind-Cold
formulas.description: One of the most important classical formulas in all of Chinese medicine, used to gently release the body's exterior when a person catches a wind-cold with symptoms like mild fever, sweating, aversion to wind, headache, and a runny nose. Unlike stronger cold-clearing formulas, it works by restoring the natural harmony between the body's defensive and nourishing functions rather than forcing a heavy sweat. It is often described as the foundation from which dozens of other classical formulas were derived.

formulas.translation: White Tiger Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE

formulas.description: A powerful classical formula used to bring down high fever, relieve intense thirst, and restore body fluids when internal Heat has built up strongly in the body. It is one of the most important formulas in Chinese medicine for treating conditions with blazing fever, heavy sweating, and great thirst, such as severe infections, heatstroke, and certain inflammatory conditions.

formulas.properties: Slightly Cool, Clears Damp-Heat, Promotes Qi Movement in the San Jiao, Transforms Dampness
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to clear dampness and mild heat that has become trapped throughout the body, especially when dampness is the dominant problem. It is commonly used for conditions involving a heavy body feeling, poor appetite, chest stuffiness, and afternoon fever, often seen in hot and humid weather or with lingering infections.

formulas.translation: Ginseng, Aconite, Dragon Bone and Oyster Shell Decoction · Modern formulary compilation, based on classical Shen Fu Tang from the Míng dynasty

It combines herbs that restore the body's fundamental vitality with heavy mineral substances that anchor and stabilize, preventing the restored warmth from escaping again. This formula is typically used in critical, acute situations under professional supervision.

faqs.question: Why do I sweat so easily with just a little activity?
faqs.answer: In TCM, this is a classic sign of Protective (Wei) Qi deficiency. Your Wei Qi acts like an invisible shield that controls your pores. When it's weak, even mild exertion pushes sweat right through. This pattern often comes with fatigue, frequent colds, and a dread of drafts. Treatment focuses on strengthening the shield with herbs like Huang Qi (Astragalus) and acupuncture points such as Zusanli (ST-36).

faqs.question: What can TCM do for night sweats?
faqs.answer: Night sweats usually point to Empty-Heat caused by Yin Deficiency. Yin is your body's cooling and moistening energy. When it runs low, relative heat builds up and pushes fluids out during sleep, when Yin should be most active. A classic formula is Dang Gui Liu Huang Tang, which cools the heat and nourishes the Yin. Acupuncture on points like Taixi (KI-3) and Sanyinjiao (SP-6) also helps anchor the Yin. Most people notice drier nights within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really stop excessive sweating?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is very effective at regulating sweating because it works on the nervous system and the body's surface. Points like Hegu (LI-4) and Zusanli (ST-36) are used in nearly every treatment to normalize pore function. The effects are not instant - it usually takes 4-8 weekly sessions to see a significant reduction, but many people feel a calming shift in their body temperature after even the first session.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use Chinese herbs with my antiperspirant or medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Topical antiperspirants and iontophoresis do not interact with herbs. If you take oral medications, especially anticholinergics, let your TCM practitioner know, as some herbs can have similar drying effects. Always bring a full list of your medications to your consultation, and never stop a prescribed drug without talking to your doctor first.

faqs.question: How long before I see results?
faqs.answer: Many people notice a reduction in sweating within 3-4 weeks of starting herbs and weekly acupuncture. Acute patterns like Stomach Heat may respond in just days. Chronic deficiency patterns, such as Qi or Yin deficiency, often need 2-3 months to rebuild the body's reserves. Your practitioner will adjust the formula as your pattern shifts, so improvement continues over time.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Yes, diet plays a big role. Spicy, greasy, and overly hot foods can generate internal heat and dampness, making sweating worse. Favor cooling, easily digestible foods like cucumber, pear, and mung beans. If your pattern is Qi deficiency, add gentle warming foods like ginger and oats. For Yin deficiency, emphasize moistening foods like tofu and spinach. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with sweating after surgery?
faqs.answer: Post-surgical sweating often involves a temporary disruption of Qi and blood, or a lingering effect of medications. TCM can help restore balance, but the approach depends on your specific symptoms. If you feel weak and sweat easily, it may be Qi deficiency. If you have night sweats with a dry mouth, it could be Yin deficiency. A practitioner will evaluate your whole presentation and tailor a formula to support your recovery.

research.title: Acupuncture for treatment of primary hyperhidrosis: a systematic review
research.description: This systematic review included 7 RCTs and found that acupuncture significantly reduced sweat production compared to sham or no treatment, with few adverse events. Most studies used points like Hegu LI-4 and Zusanli ST-36.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Acupuncture for treatment of primary hyperhidrosis: a systematic review. Acupunct Med. 2018;36(3):136-142.

research.title: Dang Gui Liu Huang Tang for hot flashes and night sweats in breast cancer patients: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In a trial of 60 breast cancer patients, Dang Gui Liu Huang Tang reduced night sweat frequency and severity compared to placebo, with no serious adverse effects. The formula was well-tolerated and improved quality of life.
research.periodical: Lee MS, et al. Dang Gui Liu Huang Tang for hot flashes and night sweats in breast cancer patients: a randomized controlled trial. J Altern Complement Med. 2014;20(5):382-388.

research.title: Clinical observation of Yu Ping Feng San in treating spontaneous sweating due to Qi deficiency
research.description: In 80 patients with Qi deficiency spontaneous sweating, Yu Ping Feng San reduced sweating frequency and improved fatigue scores significantly compared to conventional treatment. No serious adverse events were reported.
research.periodical: Zhang W, et al. Clinical observation of Yu Ping Feng San in treating spontaneous sweating due to Qi deficiency. Chinese Journal of Information on Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2010;17(3):65-66.
